title: The agents’ identity: ZDR org, GitHub App, Vault

story: Before the first agent exists, you make a list of every identity that could act in our name. Vault, our secret store, is the obvious place to start, because the Anthropic keys and the GitHub App's private key will live there. You search the org for the name of the login role that CI jobs use, gha-runners, and find a surprise: any GitHub Actions job, in any RhinoHealth repo, can log in to Vault with that role and receive the admin policy, which can read every secret we have.

Today only thirteen workflow files use the role, and our own engineers wrote all of them. Next month there will be a new repo for the agent platform, agents pushing branches to fcp, and a public repo of agent skills. Each of them would be one line of YAML away from reading every key we own, including the ones we are about to create for the agents.
hook.question: How do we give each agent, and each job around it, an identity that can do exactly its work and nothing more?

read.h: Who is asking? A signed note from GitHub
p: A CI job has no password for Vault. Instead, when a workflow has the permission id-token: write, the job can ask GitHub for an OIDC token: a JWT, a small JSON document that GitHub signs, which says where the job is running. Each fact in it is called a claim. sub says the repo and the ref, for example repo:RhinoHealth/fcp:ref:refs/heads/main. repository says the repo. job_workflow_ref names the exact workflow file the job runs, with its ref. Vault checks GitHub's signature, so nobody can forge a claim, and then it compares the claims with the role the job asks for.

A role's bound claims are the claims a token must have to log in. That one setting decides how wide the door is. gha-runners binds sub to the pattern repo:RhinoHealth/*, and the star matches anything, slashes and colons included. So every repo in the org passes, the new ones too: in the lab, jobs in the agent platform repo and the public skills repo both get admin. The fix binds a different claim instead, job_workflow_ref, to the list of workflow files that really use the role today. Because that claim names the file the job runs in, a reusable workflow matches whoever calls it, which is how fcp's integration tests use it. Below is what four jobs get from the narrowed role in the lab: only fcp's integration tests still log in.

notes.text: @* at the end allows any branch, because fcp's integration tests run on every branch push.
glob means the star in each pattern is a wildcard. With string, the patterns would have to match letter for letter.
The Terraform provider for Vault splits this string on the commas and sends Vault a list, so the job passes if any one pattern matches.
The policy stays admin in this change. Replacing it is a separate, follow-up change.

read.see:
--- RhinoHealth/fcp _cloud-int-tests-reusable-qa.yml
[admin default]
--- RhinoHealth/ai-agents nova-ci.yml
* error validating claims: claim "job_workflow_ref" does not match any associated bound claim values
--- RhinoHealth/agent-skills release.yml
* error validating claims: claim "job_workflow_ref" does not match any associated bound claim values
--- someone-else/fork release.yml
* error validating claims: claim "job_workflow_ref" does not match any associated bound claim values

p: Notice what the change does not do. The thirteen workflows still receive the admin policy, so an integration test job can still read the Anthropic keys. Making that policy smaller, one role per group of workflows with only the paths it needs, is the right end state, but it touches every job that uses Vault, and a mistake there breaks the integration tests for every engineer. So the work is split. This change only closes the door to everyone else. A person runs the plan and apply over the VPN, reruns one job per repo to prove nobody legitimate lost access, and opens the follow-up for the smaller policies.

The narrow role is also not perfect, and it helps to know where. The patterns end in a star, so a new file named _cloud-int-tests-reusable-anything.yml, pushed to any branch of fcp, would match. The lab shows it. What keeps that file out is a different wall: adding a workflow file needs a person's review once main is protected, and the agents' GitHub App has no permission to touch workflow files at all.

The same thinking applies to Claude. Imagine one Anthropic key shared by everything: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent; the routines, which are Nova started by an event such as a red build; and the brain bot, our Slack bot that answers questions from the team's documentation. One night the brain bot starts looping and spends money every second. To stop it you revoke the key, and Nova and every routine stop too. The next morning the bill shows one number, and nobody can say which agent spent it.

So the agents get their own Anthropic API organization, set up for zero data retention, or ZDR, which means Anthropic keeps no prompts and no answers from these calls. Inside it there is one workspace per workload: nova, routines and brain-bot. A workload is one kind of agent with its own key, its own meter and its own off switch. Each workspace gets exactly one key, named like nova-gateway-202610 so a rotation is visible in the name, and every key goes straight into Vault, typed in once by a DevOps admin and never pasted into a ticket, a chat or a file. Only one service ever reads them: the LLM gateway, a small service that adds the right key to each model call and counts its cost, which a later lesson builds.

code.file: run once by a DevOps admin on the VPN (trimmed)
code.text:
SECRET=infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic
for workload in nova routines brain-bot; do
  read -r -s -p "Anthropic API key for ${workload}: " key; echo
  # "=-" reads the value from stdin: the key never shows in the process list or the shell history
  printf '%s' "$key" | vault kv patch -mount=kvv2 "$SECRET" "${workload}=-"
  unset key
done
vault kv metadata put -mount=kvv2 \
  -custom-metadata=reader=llm-gateway -custom-metadata=rotate_every=90d "$SECRET"

notes.text: -s hides the key while it is typed, so it is not on the screen either.
One field per workload under one path. patch adds a field without touching the others (the very first write uses put).
The metadata says who may read the secret and when it must be rotated, so the record lives next to the key.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what the ZDR decision covers
p: Security decides the org's setup with DevOps before any key exists. The agents' org is separate from the one people use for Claude Code, because an organization that is set up for HIPAA work and one that is set up for zero data retention cannot be the same org. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 are available under ZDR. Fable is not, because it needs thirty days of data retention, and it stays off for people too until compliance decides otherwise. Anthropic's hosted Managed Agents and Claude Code cloud sessions are not allowed under ZDR, which is one reason our agents run Claude Code and the Agent SDK on our own machines in AWS. The Batch API stays off, except for evaluation data with no patient data and Security's explicit yes.

One gap is written down for the threat model instead of fixed here. On our internal cluster, the shared store that copies secrets from Vault into Kubernetes can read the whole kvv2 mount, so any ExternalSecret in any namespace could ask for these keys. The lesson on Vault and ExternalSecrets showed the fix: a store for the agents' namespace whose Vault login can read only the agents' paths.

read.h: An agent is not a person
p: The third identity is the one agents use on GitHub. You met it in the lesson on GitHub Apps: every agent pushes and opens pull requests as one private App, rhino-ai-agents, so GitHub shows rhino-ai-agents[bot] and every rule can tell agent work from a person's. Its settings are a reviewed file in the platform repo. It may write code and pull requests, and read checks and Actions, and nothing else: no administration, no members, and no workflows permission, which is what makes GitHub refuse any push from it that touches .github/workflows. It is installed on fcp only, its private key goes into Vault and the downloaded file is deleted, and it is never on the ruleset's bypass list.

Put the three together and the pattern is the same each time. Ask what the identity is bound to, and make that the smallest thing that still does the job: thirteen workflow files instead of every repo, one workload instead of every agent, one App with a short permission list instead of a person's token.

lab.title: Narrow a Vault role that trusts every repo
needs: About 500 MB of disk for the Vault image
lab.goal: Log in to a local Vault the way a GitHub Actions job does, see that today's role lets any repo in the org become admin, and bind it to a short list of workflow files.

guess.q: A Vault role binds sub to repo:RhinoHealth/* with glob matching. A job in a brand-new repo, RhinoHealth/agent-skills, asks to log in. What happens?

options.text: Refused, because the role was written before the repo existed.
options.why: Vault compares the claims at login time. The pattern matches any repo name, including ones created later.

options.text: Allowed: its sub starts with repo:RhinoHealth/, so the star matches the rest.
options.why: The glob star matches anything, so every repo in the org, today's and tomorrow's, gets the role and its policy.

options.text: Allowed only if the job runs on main.
options.why: The pattern says nothing about the branch, so any ref matches.

follow.say: Start a Vault dev server in Docker. Dev mode keeps everything in memory and gives you a root token called root, which is fine for a lab and never for real secrets.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/scratch/g0-2 && cd ~/academy-labs/scratch/g0-2 && docker run -d --name vault-lab -p 8200:8200 hashicorp/vault:1.20.4 server -dev -dev-root-token-id=root -dev-listen-address=0.0.0.0:8200

follow.say: Make a small helper, v, that runs the vault command inside the container, so you do not have to install Vault.
follow.do:
v() { docker exec -i -e VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 -e VAULT_TOKEN="${VT:-root}" vault-lab vault "$@"; }
v status | head -4
follow.see:
Key             Value
---             -----
Seal Type       shamir
Initialized     true

follow.say: Store three fake workload keys the way the real script does, from stdin, and an admin policy like the one gha-runners hands out.
follow.do:
v secrets enable -path=kvv2 kv-v2
printf '%s' sk-ant-lab-nova | v kv put -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic nova=- > /dev/null
for w in routines brain-bot; do printf '%s' "sk-ant-lab-$w" | v kv patch -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic "$w=-" > /dev/null; done
printf 'path "*" {\n  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list", "sudo"]\n}\n' | v policy write admin -
v kv get -mount=kvv2 -format=json infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic | jq .data.data
follow.see:
Success! Enabled the kv-v2 secrets engine at: kvv2/
Success! Uploaded policy: admin
{
  "brain-bot": "sk-ant-lab-brain-bot",
  "nova": "sk-ant-lab-nova",
  "routines": "sk-ant-lab-routines"
}

follow.say: GitHub signs real OIDC tokens with its own key. Make a lab key pair and a script that writes a token with the same claims a GitHub job gets.
follow.see:
writing RSA key
{
  iss: 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com',
  aud: 'https://github.com/RhinoHealth',
  sub: 'repo:RhinoHealth/agent-skills:ref:refs/heads/main',
  repository: 'RhinoHealth/agent-skills',
  job_workflow_ref: 'RhinoHealth/agent-skills/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main',
  …
}

follow.say: Tell Vault to trust tokens signed by that key, and create the role exactly as it is today.
follow.do:
v auth enable jwt
v write auth/jwt/config jwt_validation_pubkeys="$(cat github-oidc-lab.pub)" bound_issuer=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
cat > role-today.json <<'EOF'
{
  "role_type": "jwt",
  "user_claim": "sub",
  "bound_audiences": ["https://github.com/RhinoHealth"],
  "bound_claims_type": "glob",
  "bound_claims": { "sub": "repo:RhinoHealth/*" },
  "token_policies": ["admin"],
  "token_ttl": 3600
}
EOF
v write auth/jwt/role/gha-runners - < role-today.json
follow.see:
Success! Enabled jwt auth method at: jwt/
Success! Data written to: auth/jwt/config
Success! Data written to: auth/jwt/role/gha-runners

follow.say: Log in as four different jobs: fcp's integration tests, a workflow in the new agent platform repo, one in the public skills repo, and one from another org.
follow.do:
login() { echo "--- $1 $2"; v write -field=token_policies auth/jwt/login role=gha-runners jwt="$(node mint-oidc.mjs "$1" "$2" "$3")" 2>&1 | grep -E 'admin|claim'; }
login RhinoHealth/fcp _cloud-int-tests-reusable-qa.yml refs/heads/feature/rh-1234
login RhinoHealth/ai-agents nova-ci.yml
login RhinoHealth/agent-skills release.yml
login someone-else/fork release.yml
follow.see:
--- RhinoHealth/fcp _cloud-int-tests-reusable-qa.yml
[admin default]
--- RhinoHealth/ai-agents nova-ci.yml
[admin default]
--- RhinoHealth/agent-skills release.yml
[admin default]
--- someone-else/fork release.yml
* error validating claims: claim "sub" does not match any associated bound claim values

follow.say: Now see what that means: use the skills repo's login to read a key.
follow.do: VT=$(v write -field=token auth/jwt/login role=gha-runners jwt="$(node mint-oidc.mjs RhinoHealth/agent-skills release.yml)") v kv get -mount=kvv2 -field=nova infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic

lab.build: Write role-narrow.json: the same role, but bound_claims binds job_workflow_ref (not sub) to a JSON list of patterns for the files that really use the role. Use the three fcp integration-test patterns from the lesson, RhinoHealth/infrastructure/.github/workflows/ansible-molecule-test.yml@* and RhinoHealth/gitops/.github/workflows/update-rhino-client-version-staging.yml@*. Through Vault's own API the value must be a JSON list; the comma-separated string is a convenience of the Terraform provider. Apply it with v write auth/jwt/role/gha-runners - < role-narrow.json and run the four logins again.
checks: The fcp integration-test login still prints [admin default].
The ai-agents and agent-skills logins now print an error that says job_workflow_ref does not match.
Reading the nova key with the agent-skills login now fails, because there is no login.
v read -format=json auth/jwt/role/gha-runners | jq .data.bound_claims shows job_workflow_ref with a list of patterns and no sub.
lab.fix: A teammate copies your role but sets bound_claims_type to string, "because these are just strings". Make that change in a copy (jq '.bound_claims_type = "string"' role-narrow.json > role-string.json), apply it, and log in as fcp's integration tests: the job that should work is refused. Explain why, put glob back, and then try one more login, node mint-oidc.mjs RhinoHealth/fcp _cloud-int-tests-reusable-anything.yml refs/heads/sneaky. Say which wall stops someone from adding that file. When you are done, remove the container with docker rm -f vault-lab.
explain: Why does binding sub to repo:RhinoHealth/* give the role to repos that did not exist when it was written?
Why is job_workflow_ref a better claim to bind than repository for fcp's reusable integration-test workflows?
The narrow role still hands out the admin policy. Why is that left for a follow-up change, and what does the follow-up do?
lab.done: Only the fcp integration-test login gets a Vault token, the three others are refused with a claim error, and the vault-lab container is removed.

check.q: Why bind the Vault role to the list of workflow files instead of to repo:RhinoHealth/*?

options.text: Because Vault's glob matching does not support a star after a slash.
options.why: It does: the star matches slashes too, which is exactly why the old pattern let every repo in.

options.text: So that a new repo, or a new workflow in any repo, cannot log in just by asking; only the files that really use the role can.
options.why: The identity should be bound to the smallest thing that does the job. New callers then need a reviewed change to the list.

options.text: Because job_workflow_ref is shorter, so tokens are smaller.
options.why: Length has nothing to do with it. The claim decides who can get in.

check.q: At night the brain bot loops and spends money fast. With one key per workload, what does the on-call person do?

options.text: Revoke the brain-bot key; Nova and the routines keep working on their own keys.
options.why: That is the point of one key per workload: each agent has its own off switch and its own meter.

options.text: Revoke the shared Anthropic key and create a new one in the morning.
options.why: There is no shared key any more. Revoking one would stop every agent, which is the problem the split avoids.

options.text: Nothing can be done until the monthly limit is reached.
options.why: A key can be revoked at once. Limits are a separate, far-away safety net.

check.q: The agents' GitHub App has no workflows permission. How does that help the Vault role you narrowed?

options.text: It does not; the two are unrelated.
options.why: They are related: the narrow role trusts workflow file names, so who can add workflow files matters.

options.text: It makes Vault refuse tokens from bot accounts.
options.why: Vault never sees the App. It only sees the OIDC token of the job.

options.text: A fooled agent cannot add a workflow file whose name matches one of the role's patterns, because GitHub refuses the push.
options.why: The patterns end in a star, so a new file with a matching name would get in. The missing permission is the wall that keeps agents from creating one.

p: Security (Ronen, with DevOps) decides the ZDR org; DevOps creates it with the Anthropic account team, makes the workspaces nova, routines and brain-bot with one key each, and stores them at kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/anthropic with reader=llm-gateway and a 90-day rotation reminder. The gap that the inf ClusterSecretStore vault-store can read all of kvv2 goes to the G3 threat model.

The App rhino-ai-agents is created from ai-agents/settings/github-app.json, installed on RhinoHealth/fcp only (ai-agents is added when dogfooding starts), and its key lives at kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/github-app, read only by the broker. The gha-runners change lives in infrastructure/modules/vault/auth_backends.tf and must land before any agent workflow exists.

A known gap: the narrowed patterns end in -*.yml@*, so a new fcp workflow file named like _cloud-int-tests-reusable-x.yml on any branch still gets admin. Branch protection and the App's missing workflows permission cover agents, but a person with write access could add one on a branch; the follow-up least-privilege roles are what really shrink this.

tickets.why: The ZDR org decision: separate org, allowed models, Fable and Batch API off, admins and workloads named.
One workspace and one key per workload, stored only in Vault with the stdin script.
The rhino-ai-agents GitHub App: short permission list, fcp only, key in Vault, no bypass.
Bind gha-runners to job_workflow_ref for the 13 real callers; the least-privilege policies are the follow-up.

words.plain: A short-lived JSON document that GitHub signs for one CI job, saying which repo, ref and workflow file it runs.
One fact inside a signed token, such as sub or job_workflow_ref.
The claims a token must have to log in with a Vault role. They decide how wide the door is.
One kind of agent (nova, routines, brain-bot) with its own key, meter and off switch.
Zero data retention: the provider keeps no prompts and no answers from these API calls.

review.q: Explain to a teammate what sub and job_workflow_ref contain, and why the role binds the second one.
review.a: sub holds repo and ref (repo:Org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main); job_workflow_ref holds the exact workflow file and its ref. Binding the file list means only the workflows that really use the role can log in, and reusable workflows match whoever calls them.

review.q: Why one Anthropic key per workload instead of one key for all agents?
review.a: Each workload gets its own meter and its own off switch: revoking one key stops one agent. A shared key would stop everything and hide who spent what.

review.q: The narrowed role still gives admin. What is the next step, and why was it not done in the same change?
review.a: One role per group of workflows with a least-privilege policy (I&T reads QA secrets only, and so on). It touches every Vault user and could break the integration tests, so it is a separate, reviewed change after the door to everyone else is closed.

remember: Ask what each identity is bound to, and bind it to the smallest thing that still does the job: listed workflow files, one workload, one App with a short permission list.
